apogee

AP-uh-jee · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Apogee is the highest point of development, success, or achievement in something's growth or history.

Paleontologists mark the mid-Jurassic as the apogee of long-necked dinosaur diversity, a high-water mark the group's numbers would never again match.

Example

The band's sold-out world tour marked the apogee of their career, a peak they would spend the rest of their lives trying to recapture.

Apogee describes the highest point in a process that has been building up over time -- it almost always implies there was a rise beforehand, and often a decline after.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

peak: A peak is any highest point or level -- a mountain peak, peak traffic, the peak of a fever. It is a plain maximum with no story attached. An apogee always tells a story: a long rise that finally crested, usually with a decline to follow.

culmination: A culmination is the finishing point a process has been building toward -- the moment everything comes together and is complete. An apogee is a high-water mark, not a finish: a career can sail past its apogee and keep going, downhill.

heyday: A heyday is a golden stretch of time -- the years when something was at its most successful and popular. It names an era, not an instant. An apogee is the single topmost point inside such a story, the one moment the long rise actually crested.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

nadir: the lowest point in someone's fortunes

trough: a low point, especially in a repeating pattern

Where it sits · how supreme the peak is — high point → apogee → pinnacle

high point vs. apogee: A high point is a general phrase for any good moment, without apogee's sense of a long historical or developmental buildup.

pinnacle vs. apogee: Pinnacle sits above apogee on this scale: it claims the very top of the top, the most impressive summit imaginable, while an apogee is only the highest point of its own particular story.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — apo-

prefix — apo-: away from (Greek apo, 'away from, off')

root — -gee

root — -gee: earth (Greek ge, 'earth')

Put it together

Put it together: Apogee comes from Greek apo- ('away from') + ge ('earth') -- literally 'away from earth,' an astronomy term for the point in an orbit farthest from Earth, which came to mean any high point in a long development.

Use the root in a new word: geography

Use the root in a new word: geography: Geography -- literally 'earth-writing' -- shares apogee's Greek root ge, meaning 'earth.'
